title: One Online Order
subtitle: Buy Now to the doorstep
learningObjective: Map the process, find the decisions, judge whether AI fits, and design only the decisions that survive.
throughline: Hunt for the diamonds — that is where AI replaces judgment.

introduction.title: What happens after a customer selects Buy Now?
introduction.context: An online order looks like one transaction to the customer, but fulfilling it crosses commerce, fraud operations, warehouse, carrier, and support teams. Each handoff can change whether the order is accepted, where inventory is sourced, what delivery promise is made, and how an exception is resolved.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one order through address and payment checks, inventory and carrier assignment, picking and packing, delivery monitoring, and customer support. The exception paths reveal the manual review, oversold inventory, late-delivery, and remedy work hidden behind the normal path.
introduction.startsWhen: The customer submits items, delivery details, payment, and account context.
introduction.endsWhen: The order is delivered and kept, or its final exception and remedy are resolved.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Items, address, card, account history

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Verify, allocate stock, pick, pack, label

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Is this payment good? Which carrier?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Ship, hold for review, or cancel

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: It arrived Thursday, and they kept it

decisions.label: Is this address deliverable?
decisions.wrongCost: A parcel goes nowhere
decisions.testAnswer: No. Another year of data does not change a published postal rule.
decisions.why: The format and service-area logic are stable and known in advance.
decisions.recommendation: Implement deterministic validation and address correction, not a model.

decisions.label: Is this payment fraudulent?
decisions.wrongCost: A chargeback, or a good customer lost
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. New outcomes reveal changing fraud patterns that nobody has fully written down.
decisions.why: The decision depends on patterns across many prior examples and changes as fraud tactics move.
decisions.recommendation: Rank payments into approve, review, and decline buckets; route ambiguity to an analyst.

data.summary: Three years of orders and final outcomes, not only analyst approvals.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: owned, labelled, refreshing
data.risk: Historical labels record what analysts decided, not necessarily what was true.

method.technique: Explainable gradient-boosted classifier on tabular features

metric.technical: Catch 85% of currently detected fraud while sending under 3% of good orders to review.
metric.business: Halve 83 monthly review hours without increasing chargebacks or rejecting good customers.
metric.baseline: 40,000 orders × 3.1% flagged × 4 minutes = 83 staff-hours per month

human.checkpoint: Review genuinely ambiguous payments with evidence and enough time to decide.
human.falsePositiveCost: A legitimate customer is blocked and may not return.
human.falseNegativeCost: Fraud succeeds; the retailer loses goods, payment, and a chargeback fee.

decisions.label: Will it arrive when promised?
decisions.wrongCost: A broken promise and a support ticket
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Weather, seasonal volume, route, and carrier performance change with new data.
decisions.why: The outcome is uncertain and must be estimated from historical delivery results.
decisions.recommendation: Predict the probability or expected delay, then surface risk before promising a date.

data.summary: Historical promised and actual delivery times joined to route conditions.
data.readiness: Cross-team data; expect ownership and integration work
data.risk: Averages hide the expensive late tail; actual outcomes must be captured consistently.

method.output: Expected arrival or probability of missing the promise
method.technique: Supervised delivery-time prediction with calibrated uncertainty

metric.technical: MAE or RMSE in delivery days, plus performance on the worst 5% of misses.
metric.business: Reduce broken promises and related support tickets from the 1.8% late baseline.
metric.baseline: 1.8% of orders delivered late under the synthetic baseline

human.checkpoint: Set acceptable risk thresholds and review persistent carrier or route failures.
human.falsePositiveCost: An unnecessarily conservative promise may reduce conversion.
human.falseNegativeCost: A confident but late promise creates support cost and lost trust.

decisions.label: Which warehouse, which carrier?
decisions.wrongCost: Extra freight cost, or a late delivery
decisions.testAnswer: No training data is required if the objective and constraints can be written exactly.
decisions.why: This is an assignment problem with costs, capacity, inventory, service levels, and routes.
decisions.recommendation: Use an operations-research solver before considering machine learning.

decisions.label: What do we tell an unhappy customer?
decisions.wrongCost: Churn, or a refund the retailer never owed
decisions.testAnswer: The policy decision stays separate; generation can draft the communication from grounded facts.
decisions.why: Generation produces an artifact inside a process box rather than resolving the policy diamond.
decisions.recommendation: Ground a draft in actual order status and policy, then require agent review before sending.

data.summary: Current order, tracking events, approved policy, prior contact, and tone guidance.
data.readiness: Operational sources exist but must be joined and permissioned
data.risk: A fluent draft can still invent status, policy, or compensation.

method.technique: Retrieval-grounded text generation with policy and order tools

metric.business: Human acceptance rate, response time, repeat contacts, and avoidable refunds.
metric.baseline: About 900 monthly support cases in the synthetic baseline

human.checkpoint: Verify facts, policy, tone, and remedy before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The system offers compensation or makes a promise that policy does not support.
human.falseNegativeCost: The response omits a real issue and the customer contacts support again.

decisions.label: Refund, replace, or deny?
decisions.wrongCost: Margin, or a customer who never returns
decisions.testAnswer: The costs are lopsided and the judgment combines policy, context, and customer impact.
decisions.why: A model can prepare evidence, but it should not own the consequential remedy decision in this first design.
decisions.recommendation: Improve the evidence shown to the support lead; keep final authority with the human.

title: One Equipment Alert
subtitle: From noisy signal to safe return to service
learningObjective: Separate signal validation, failure prediction, inspection prioritization, diagnostic support, and accountable equipment action.
throughline: A risk score can focus attention; it cannot authorize a shutdown.

introduction.title: Why one machine alert becomes a cross-team decision
introduction.context: Industrial equipment produces a steady stream of alarms and sensor readings, but many alerts are duplicates, noise, or signs that do not require immediate intervention. Reliability and maintenance teams must identify real failure risk, use scarce technicians and parts well, and protect production without allowing a prediction to control equipment directly.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one alert through signal validation, asset-history enrichment, 48-hour failure-risk estimation, inspection prioritization, work-order creation, field diagnosis, and an accountable decision to monitor, repair, run at reduced output, or stop the equipment.
introduction.startsWhen: A monitored machine produces an alert that may indicate changing equipment condition.
introduction.endsWhen: The alert is closed as noise, the asset remains under monitoring, or repair is verified and the asset is safe to operate.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Telemetry, asset history, operating context

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Validate, enrich, triage, inspect

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Failure risk? Inspect first? Stop equipment?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Monitor, diagnose, repair, or shut down

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Safe availability with fewer surprise stops

decisions.label: Is this signal valid?
decisions.wrongCost: Wasted inspection capacity, or a real warning discarded
decisions.testAnswer: No. Range checks, stale timestamps, duplicate windows, and sensor-health flags are known validation logic.
decisions.why: The cheapest first step is deterministic validation before any learned pattern is trusted.
decisions.recommendation: Apply sensor-health, freshness, range, and duplicate-event rules; route unresolved quality failures for instrumentation repair.

decisions.label: Will this asset fail within 48 hours?
decisions.wrongCost: An unnecessary interruption, or an unplanned production stop
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Confirmed outcomes reveal changing combinations of vibration, temperature, load, and prior repair history.
decisions.why: The output is the calibrated probability of a future event over a defined time horizon.
decisions.recommendation: Estimate 48-hour failure risk with uncertainty and evidence; never connect the score directly to equipment control.

data.summary: Time-aligned telemetry joined to asset configuration, maintenance actions, and confirmed failure outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: 18 months available; failure labels require review
data.risk: Work orders record what technicians did, not always the true failure mode; leakage from post-failure signals can inflate results.

method.output: Probability of confirmed failure within 48 hours
method.technique: Calibrated supervised prediction over engineered time-window features

metric.technical: Calibration error and recall at the inspection-capacity threshold, segmented by asset class.
metric.business: Increase useful inspections and reduce the six monthly unplanned stops without increasing unnecessary shutdowns.
metric.baseline: 1,800 alerts, 140 inspections, and 6 unplanned stops per month

human.checkpoint: Review evidence, uncertainty, operating context, and recent maintenance before recommending action.
human.falsePositiveCost: A healthy asset consumes scarce inspection time or is interrupted unnecessarily.
human.falseNegativeCost: A failure is missed and causes safety exposure, downtime, or secondary damage.

decisions.label: Which asset should be inspected first?
decisions.wrongCost: A high-impact asset waits while capacity is spent elsewhere
decisions.testAnswer: The inputs may include predictions, but the choice is an allocation problem with technicians, parts, access windows, and production impact.
decisions.why: A stated objective and explicit constraints are more transparent than asking a model to imitate historical schedules.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize the inspection queue using risk, consequence, capacity, access, skills, and parts constraints.

decisions.label: Should a work order be opened?
decisions.wrongCost: Duplicate work and queue noise, or an approved task never reaches a technician
decisions.testAnswer: No. Once required evidence, priority, and duplicate checks pass, the handoff is deterministic.
decisions.why: This is controlled workflow automation, not a judgment that improves by learning from examples.
decisions.recommendation: Create a work order only after required fields, duplicate, authorization, and scheduling checks pass.

decisions.label: What should the technician check next?
decisions.wrongCost: Longer diagnosis, an unsafe instruction, or a missed root cause
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can assemble a context-specific diagnostic brief, but the technician must validate it against the asset and safety procedure.
decisions.why: The output is a grounded work artifact, not the final equipment decision.
decisions.recommendation: Draft evidence-linked checks from current signals, manuals, prior repairs, and approved procedures for technician review.

data.summary: Current alert evidence, asset manual, approved safety procedures, prior work orders, and known-failure guidance.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: manuals are approved; work-order notes vary in quality
data.risk: A fluent diagnostic sequence can omit lockout requirements or repeat an incorrect historical repair.

method.output: Evidence-linked diagnostic brief and suggested check sequence
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation with asset, procedure, and work-history tools

metric.technical: Grounded claim rate, required-safety-step coverage, and unsupported-instruction rate.
metric.business: Reduce first-diagnosis time and repeat visits without increasing safety deviations or unnecessary parts use.
metric.baseline: 140 monthly inspections with technician review required for every brief

human.checkpoint: Confirm asset identity, lockout requirements, observed condition, and each diagnostic action before execution.
human.falsePositiveCost: The technician performs an irrelevant or disruptive check.
human.falseNegativeCost: The brief omits a critical cause or safety step and the asset returns to service incorrectly.

decisions.label: Should operations stop the equipment?
decisions.frequency: Only when evidence indicates consequential risk
decisions.wrongCost: Production is interrupted unnecessarily, or unsafe equipment continues running
decisions.testAnswer: No model should own this consequential action. The decision combines evidence, safety procedure, production state, and accountable authority.
decisions.why: Predictions and diagnostic evidence inform the decision, but they do not carry operational accountability.
decisions.recommendation: Present evidence and escalation criteria; require an authorized supervisor to stop, derate, or continue operation.

title: One Customer Identity (KYC) Review
subtitle: From customer submission to accountable case disposition
learningObjective: Separate document interpretation, explicit policy checks, screening triage, workflow automation, and accountable compliance judgment.
throughline: AI can prepare and triage evidence; policy stays explicit and disposition stays human.

introduction.title: What a customer identity review is protecting
introduction.context: Know Your Customer, or KYC, is the regulated process used to verify who a customer is, understand beneficial ownership, and identify evidence that requires additional review before an account is opened. The work combines variable documents with explicit policy, screening requirements, and decisions that can materially affect both the institution and the applicant.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one onboarding packet through document extraction, identity and ownership normalization, completeness and consistency checks, approved screening, review routing, and human disposition. Low-confidence evidence, missing documents, conflicting records, and uncertain screening matches create the exception paths.
introduction.startsWhen: An applicant submits identity, onboarding, and ownership evidence.
introduction.endsWhen: An authorized compliance role records a clear, escalate, or decline disposition with supporting evidence.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Identity documents, forms, ownership, policy

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Intake, extract, normalize, screen

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Reliable? Complete? Consistent? Potential match?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Clear, request evidence, or escalate

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Traceable analyst-owned disposition

decisions.label: Can the required evidence be extracted reliably?
decisions.wrongCost: Bad fields contaminate every later check, or a readable packet is delayed
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Document layouts, image quality, and field representations vary, and reviewed examples improve extraction confidence and document classification.
decisions.why: The system must classify document and field evidence while exposing uncertainty and source location.
decisions.recommendation: Extract field values with source citations and confidence; send low-confidence evidence to document review.

data.summary: Representative onboarding documents paired with reviewed field values, document classes, and extraction outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: approved sample set exists; rare layouts need coverage review
data.risk: Historical reviewer corrections may be inconsistent, and aggregate accuracy can hide weak performance on rare documents.

method.output: Document class, field values, source citations, and confidence
method.technique: Layout-aware document extraction with field-level confidence and abstention

metric.technical: Field precision, field recall, packet classification accuracy, and grounded citation rate by document type.
metric.business: Reduce 360 monthly preparation hours while keeping exception rework and incorrect straight-through packets below baseline.
metric.baseline: 5,000 packets with 24% entering 18 minutes of exception preparation

human.checkpoint: Verify low-confidence values against the source image and record corrections without deciding customer disposition.
human.falsePositiveCost: An incorrect field is treated as reliable and contaminates policy or screening checks.
human.falseNegativeCost: Usable evidence is rejected and creates avoidable applicant and analyst work.

decisions.label: Are all policy-required fields present?
decisions.wrongCost: An incomplete case advances, or an applicant is asked for evidence that is not required
decisions.testAnswer: No. Versioned policy defines required documents and fields for each product, entity type, and jurisdiction.
decisions.why: Explicit policy checks are more transparent and auditable than learning requirements from historical analyst behavior.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate versioned completeness rules and identify every missing requirement with its policy source.

decisions.label: Do identity and ownership records agree?
decisions.wrongCost: A material conflict is missed, or harmless formatting differences create rework
decisions.testAnswer: Mostly no. Exact comparison, approved normalization, date tolerance, and ownership-total rules resolve the known cases; ambiguity should be escalated.
decisions.why: Known consistency checks should remain deterministic and explainable at field level.
decisions.recommendation: Normalize approved variants, apply explicit comparisons and tolerances, and escalate unresolved source conflicts.

decisions.label: Is this a plausible screening match?
decisions.wrongCost: A real risk is missed, or a customer is delayed by a false match
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Reviewed outcomes improve ranking across names, aliases, dates, jurisdictions, and incomplete identifiers, but uncertainty must be visible.
decisions.why: The output is a present-state match class, not a final compliance decision.
decisions.recommendation: Rank candidate matches as likely, uncertain, or unlikely with field-level comparison evidence for analyst review.

data.summary: Approved screening lists, normalized applicant identifiers, candidate pairs, and analyst-confirmed match outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: list provenance is controlled and reviewed match outcomes are retained
data.risk: Name and geography patterns can create unequal false-positive burdens; list freshness and identity resolution are critical.

method.output: Likely match, uncertain match, or unlikely match with comparison evidence
method.technique: High-recall candidate generation followed by calibrated pair classification

metric.technical: Recall of confirmed matches, false-positive rate, calibration, and subgroup review burden.
metric.business: Reduce avoidable screening review time without increasing missed confirmed matches or customer delay.
metric.baseline: All potential matches require analyst disposition under the defined review boundary

human.checkpoint: Compare source records, resolve uncertain identity evidence, and document the match rationale.
human.falsePositiveCost: A customer experiences unnecessary delay, investigation, or adverse treatment.
human.falseNegativeCost: A material screening match is missed and the institution accepts unmanaged risk.

decisions.label: Which approved review queue receives the packet?
decisions.wrongCost: A case waits in the wrong queue or bypasses required specialist review
decisions.testAnswer: No. Product, jurisdiction, issue type, risk flags, and required reviewer role define an auditable routing table.
decisions.why: Once evidence and statuses are established, queue routing is controlled execution rather than learned judgment.
decisions.recommendation: Route through versioned mappings and fail closed when no authorized destination exists.

decisions.label: Should this case be cleared, escalated, or declined?
decisions.wrongCost: The institution accepts unmanaged risk, or a customer receives an unjustified adverse outcome
decisions.testAnswer: No model should own regulated case disposition. Evidence, policy, uncertainty, customer impact, and accountable authority must remain visible.
decisions.why: AI and rules prepare the packet; an authorized officer owns the consequential conclusion and rationale.
decisions.recommendation: Require human disposition with cited evidence, policy version, conflict history, and an auditable rationale.

title: One Resident Service Request
subtitle: From everyday language to the right accountable service
learningObjective: Separate language interpretation, entitlement rules, capacity allocation, grounded communication, and accountable exception handling.
throughline: Use AI for language ambiguity, rules for entitlement, and people for accountable exceptions.

introduction.title: Why a simple resident request can be difficult to route
introduction.context: Residents describe needs in everyday language, while public services are organized by program, jurisdiction, eligibility, and provider capacity. They also carry safeguarding duties: responding quickly when a person may be at risk of harm. A wrong first route makes people repeat their story, delays support, and can hide an urgent situation that needs trained human attention.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows one request from natural-language intake through service classification, jurisdiction and eligibility checks, duplicate handling, provider assignment, resident communication, and exception review. Clarification, transfers, capacity limits, and urgent protection escalation form the main alternate paths.
introduction.startsWhen: A resident submits a request through an available intake channel.
introduction.endsWhen: The appropriate service receives a routed case with verified context, or an urgent exception is escalated and recorded.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Resident request, location, service catalog

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Interpret, verify, match, route

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Which need? Eligible? Which office? Exception?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Clarify, assign, escalate, or create case

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Resident reaches the right service with context

decisions.label: Which service need is the resident describing?
decisions.wrongCost: The resident repeats their story, loses time, or never reaches the right service
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. Reviewed requests reveal varied language, multilingual phrasing, and overlapping descriptions that improve service-category matching.
decisions.why: The output is a present-state service category with confidence, not an entitlement decision.
decisions.recommendation: Rank approved service categories, cite the phrases that drove the match, and ask a focused question when confidence is low.

data.summary: Permission-cleared request text paired with final service categories, clarification turns, language, channel, and routing outcomes.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: reviewed routing history exists; historical misroutes must not become labels
data.risk: Past routing may encode unequal access or staff shortcuts; rare needs and languages can disappear in aggregate metrics.

method.output: Ranked service categories, confidence, and a clarification question when needed
method.technique: Multilingual text classification with calibrated abstention and approved service taxonomy

metric.technical: Macro precision and recall, calibration, abstention quality, and performance by language and service category.
metric.business: Improve first-route accuracy from the 14% misroute baseline and reduce repeat explanations without suppressing escalation.
metric.baseline: 12,000 monthly requests; 19% need clarification and 14% are initially misrouted

human.checkpoint: Review uncertain or urgent requests, correct the category, and preserve the resident's original wording.
human.falsePositiveCost: A plausible but wrong category sends the resident through another avoidable transfer.
human.falseNegativeCost: The system fails to surface a relevant service or urgent need.

decisions.label: Which authority has jurisdiction?
decisions.wrongCost: A request sits with an office that cannot act
decisions.testAnswer: No. Service area, address, program ownership, and inter-agency agreements are published constraints.
decisions.why: Jurisdiction should be explicit, versioned, and explainable rather than inferred from historical transfers.
decisions.recommendation: Resolve jurisdiction through the governed service catalog and route unknown boundaries for catalog maintenance.

decisions.label: Does the request meet the stated service criteria?
decisions.wrongCost: An eligible resident is blocked, or an ineligible case consumes scarce capacity
decisions.testAnswer: No. Stated eligibility conditions and required evidence belong in policy logic, not a model trained on past approvals.
decisions.why: Rules preserve transparency, appealability, and the distinction between missing evidence and ineligibility.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate only approved criteria, show the reason and policy source, and never infer protected or missing facts.

decisions.label: Should this request update an existing open case?
decisions.wrongCost: Duplicate work is created, or unrelated residents are merged
decisions.testAnswer: No for exact identifiers and case references. Ambiguous identity matches must be reviewed rather than guessed.
decisions.why: Controlled duplicate handling is workflow execution once identity and open-case keys are established.
decisions.recommendation: Merge only on approved exact keys; present ambiguous candidates to staff without automatic consolidation.

decisions.label: Which office or provider should receive the case?
decisions.wrongCost: A resident waits while another provider has suitable capacity
decisions.testAnswer: The choice balances capacity, location, accessibility, specialization, language, and appointment constraints.
decisions.why: The assignment objective and constraints can be stated and audited directly.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize among eligible providers and expose the constraint that drove each assignment or failure to assign.

decisions.label: How should the next step be explained to the resident?
decisions.frequency: Every routed, clarified, or ineligible request
decisions.wrongCost: The resident misunderstands the next step, misses evidence, or receives an unsupported promise
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can turn grounded service facts and rule outcomes into accessible language, but staff must verify consequential guidance.
decisions.why: The output is a communication artifact inside the workflow, not the eligibility or exception decision.
decisions.recommendation: Draft a plain-language explanation from the request, cited catalog entry, rule result, and approved accessibility guidance.

data.summary: Original request, approved service descriptions, rule outcomes, required evidence, accessibility guidance, and supported languages.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: approved service content is versioned; translations require review
data.risk: A fluent message can invent eligibility, deadlines, availability, or commitments that no source supports.

method.output: Grounded next-step explanation or focused request for missing information
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation constrained to service facts and deterministic rule results

metric.technical: Groundedness, unsupported-commitment rate, required-information coverage, and accessibility review pass rate.
metric.business: Reduce repeat contacts, clarification cycles, and abandoned requests while maintaining equitable comprehension.
metric.baseline: 19% of requests currently need at least one clarification cycle

human.checkpoint: Verify service facts, rule result, tone, language, accessibility, and any requested evidence before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The message promises service, eligibility, or timing that is not supported.
human.falseNegativeCost: The message omits a required next step and forces another contact.

decisions.label: Does this request need an exception or safeguarding response?
decisions.wrongCost: A vulnerable resident is missed, or a routine case is escalated intrusively
decisions.testAnswer: No model should own discretionary exception or safeguarding action. Context, consent, policy, and accountable judgment matter.
decisions.why: AI may surface evidence, but a trained caseworker must interpret urgency and authorize exceptional handling.
decisions.recommendation: Provide the original request, source facts, rule outcomes, and escalation guidance to an accountable caseworker.

title: One Day of Fleet Dispatch
subtitle: From promised jobs to safe routes under disruption
learningObjective: Separate travel prediction, route optimization, deterministic safety checks, controlled automation, customer communication, and dispatcher authority.
throughline: Prediction estimates what may happen; optimization chooses under constraints; the dispatcher owns the risky override.

introduction.title: Why a fleet plan keeps changing after dispatch
introduction.context: Daily fleet dispatch converts customer commitments into executable vehicle routes while balancing vehicle capacity, promised delivery windows, legal driver-hour limits, vehicle condition, traffic, and weather. Even a workable morning plan can become invalid when demand exceeds capacity, a vehicle breaks down, roads change, or a delivery promise becomes unlikely to hold.
introduction.workflow: The workflow follows a day of jobs from input validation through lateness prediction, route optimization, plan approval, and execution. During disruptions it checks non-negotiable safety and legal limits, recalculates recovery options, requires a dispatcher to approve changes to service promises, and prepares evidence-based customer updates.
introduction.startsWhen: Dispatch receives the day's jobs, customer promises, available vehicles, drivers, and operating conditions.
introduction.endsWhen: Jobs are completed safely and any disruption, changed promise, or authorized tradeoff is communicated and recorded.

stages.label: Inputs
stages.description: Jobs, fleet state, traffic, weather, promises

stages.label: Process
stages.description: Validate, predict, optimize, dispatch

stages.label: Decision
stages.description: Late risk? Best route? Replan? Override?

stages.label: Action
stages.description: Release, drive, reassign, or notify

stages.label: Outcome
stages.description: Safe completion with visible service tradeoffs

decisions.label: Are jobs, locations, vehicles, and constraints valid?
decisions.wrongCost: The solver returns a route that cannot be executed
decisions.testAnswer: No. Required fields, coordinate quality, vehicle status, hours limits, and service windows are explicit checks.
decisions.why: Optimization and prediction should never receive inputs that already violate known constraints.
decisions.recommendation: Fail closed on invalid or stale inputs and show the exact field or constraint that needs repair.

decisions.label: Which jobs are likely to miss their service window?
decisions.wrongCost: A preventable late promise, or costly buffer added to every route
decisions.testAnswer: Yes. New outcomes reveal changing travel times across traffic, weather, location, season, stop sequence, and vehicle conditions.
decisions.why: The output is a calibrated probability and expected amount of future lateness over a defined route horizon.
decisions.recommendation: Predict travel time and late risk with uncertainty; pass those estimates into the route solver rather than asking the model to choose routes.

data.summary: Planned and actual arrival events joined to routes, stops, traffic, weather, vehicle, driver-hours, and service-window context.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: event timestamps exist; reason codes for dwell and failed stops need cleanup
data.risk: Completed routes exclude cancelled and failed jobs unless outcomes are joined carefully; location and shift coverage can be uneven.

method.output: Expected arrival and probability of missing each service window
method.technique: Calibrated travel-time prediction with route-context and disruption features

metric.technical: Arrival-time MAE, late-event recall, calibration, and performance on the worst 5% of misses.
metric.business: Reduce the 8.5% late-job baseline and avoidable replanning without inflating route cost or unsafe pressure on drivers.
metric.baseline: 420 daily jobs with 8.5% late and 14 disruptions requiring attention

human.checkpoint: Review drift, extreme misses, route segments, and operational changes before estimates affect service promises.
human.falsePositiveCost: An overly pessimistic estimate creates unnecessary buffer, cost, or customer concern.
human.falseNegativeCost: A confident late miss breaks a promise and leaves the dispatcher no recovery time.

decisions.label: What is the best feasible route plan?
decisions.wrongCost: Excess distance, missed windows, unserved jobs, or infeasible driver work
decisions.testAnswer: No historical imitation is required when the objective and constraints can be written explicitly.
decisions.why: This is a vehicle-routing allocation problem using predicted travel time as one input.
decisions.recommendation: Optimize cost and service subject to capacity, hours, skills, windows, safety, and vehicle constraints; expose infeasibility.

decisions.label: Can this approved route plan be released?
decisions.wrongCost: Drivers receive conflicting or unauthorized work
decisions.testAnswer: No. Release follows explicit validation, plan version, authorization, and driver acknowledgment rules.
decisions.why: This is audited execution after decisions are complete, not another model judgment.
decisions.recommendation: Publish only the latest approved feasible plan, record acknowledgments, and prevent stale-plan dispatch.

decisions.label: Can the current route continue safely?
decisions.wrongCost: An unsafe or legally invalid route continues, or a minor event triggers needless replanning
decisions.testAnswer: No for vehicle safety, driver hours, road closure, and mandatory service constraints.
decisions.why: Known legal and safety boundaries must be deterministic and fail closed.
decisions.recommendation: Evaluate hard constraints first; continue only when they pass and send the changed state to replanning otherwise.

decisions.label: What is the best feasible recovery plan?
decisions.wrongCost: The fleet recovers slowly, violates a constraint, or sacrifices the wrong commitments
decisions.testAnswer: The new state changes constraints and objective tradeoffs; the solver should recompute rather than a model inventing an action.
decisions.why: Recovery is the same constrained allocation problem with updated vehicles, jobs, times, and promises.
decisions.recommendation: Re-solve from the current state, preserve hard constraints, and present tradeoff options when no plan meets every promise.

decisions.label: What should the affected customer be told?
decisions.frequency: Every disruption that changes a promise
decisions.wrongCost: A false ETA or unsupported remedy damages trust and creates repeat contact
decisions.testAnswer: Generation can turn grounded route facts and approved policy into a clear update, but it must not invent an ETA or remedy.
decisions.why: The output is a communication artifact grounded in the approved recovery plan.
decisions.recommendation: Draft from the latest plan version, event evidence, revised ETA, service policy, and approved remedy options; require review before sending.

data.summary: Latest approved route, observed disruption, revised ETA, customer promise, communication history, and service policy.
data.readiness: Synthetic readiness assumption: route versions are controlled and approved communication policy is retrievable
data.risk: Stale route state can produce a polished but incorrect ETA or compensation promise.

method.output: Grounded disruption update with revised expectation and approved next step
method.technique: Retrieval-grounded generation constrained to the current route plan and service policy

metric.technical: Groundedness, stale-plan use, unsupported-promise rate, and required-fact coverage.
metric.business: Improve reviewer acceptance and reduce repeat contacts without increasing compensation errors or customer complaints.
metric.baseline: 14 daily disruptions create manual replanning and communication work

human.checkpoint: Verify the current plan version, ETA, customer impact, policy, and remedy before sending.
human.falsePositiveCost: The customer receives an unsupported promise, unnecessary remedy, or wrong ETA.
human.falseNegativeCost: A material delay or required next step is omitted and the customer cannot respond.

decisions.label: Should a service tradeoff or operational override be authorized?
decisions.frequency: Only when no plan satisfies every service goal
decisions.wrongCost: Safety or legal limits are breached, or a recoverable service promise is abandoned
decisions.testAnswer: Hard safety constraints are never overridable; accountable staff must own any permitted service tradeoff among feasible options.
decisions.why: The solver can expose options and consequences, but it does not carry authority for consequential operational choices.
decisions.recommendation: Block hard-constraint violations and require dispatcher rationale for any permitted customer or cost tradeoff.
